visits.text: Allow for a day trip from Amman to visit Jerash. Jerash welcomes you through Hadrian's Arch, erected in 129 for the emperor's visit—a gateway measuring 25 m by 21 m leading into one of the best-preserved Roman cities in the Near East, sometimes nicknamed the “Pompeii of the East”. Pass the hippodrome, then emerge onto the Oval Plaza, a forum measuring 90 m by 80 m and the only oval-shaped one. Its first-century Ionic colonnade encloses a space used both as a market and a gathering place. The Cardo Maximus starts here, stretching 800 meters and lined with 200 Corinthian columns—you can still see the ruts left by chariots in the paving stones. Allow 2 to 3 hours for the site and bring a hat, as there is hardly any shade.

Don't leave Jerash without pushing on to the Temple of Artemis, dedicated to the city's patron goddess. Its 12-meter Corinthian columns still rise against the sky. The South Theater, built around 90 under Domitian, seated 5,000 spectators—climb to the upper tiers and test the acoustics by clapping your hands at the center of the stage. It still serves as a performance venue during the Jerash Festival in July.

Back in Amman (~1 hour's drive), climb to the Citadel on Jebel al-Qala'a hill at an elevation of 850 meters. The Temple of Hercules, commissioned under Marcus Aurelius between 162 and 166, preserves two 10-meter columns and three stone fingers from a colossal statue—the scale becomes dizzying when you imagine the original size. Just behind it, the Umayyad Palace, built around 720 and destroyed by the earthquake of 749, has a vaulted audience hall designed to impress the governor's visitors. Go in the late afternoon: at sunset, the panorama of Amman's thousands of beige houses and the Roman theater below is the best in the city.

Walk back down to the Roman Theater, carved into the rock in the 2nd century and able to seat 6,000 spectators. From there, plunge into the Downtown souk: the lively streets connect the theater to the al-Husseini Mosque. It's the perfect spot to taste your first mansaf (lamb stew in fermented yogurt, Jordan's national dish) or a hot falafel fresh from the fryer.
Enjoy one last morning snorkeling session on the reefs south of Aqaba—King Abdullah Reef has corals in excellent condition and hawksbill turtles.

Take the road back to Amman via the Dead Sea Highway, which follows the Jordan Valley (~4 hours' driving). The road itself is a spectacle: the cliffs of Wadi Araba on the left, the desert on the right, then the bluish surface of the Dead Sea appearing below.

Before heading to the airport, devote 2 hours to the Jordan Museum in the Ras al-Ain quarter. It's the country's largest museum (10,000 m²), with collections spanning prehistory to the present. The highlights: fragments of the Dead Sea Scrolls, discovered in the Qumran caves between 1947 and 1956—including the famous Copper Scroll that describes a hidden treasure—and the Ain Ghazal statues, 9,000 years old, among the world's oldest human statues.

If time permits, take a final stroll through Jabal al-Weibdeh, right next to the museum. The Darat al Funun gallery occupies several restored traditional houses overlooking downtown, with contemporary Arab art exhibitions and pleasant gardens. Entry is free.

activities.text: Evening stroll through the Rainbow Street quarter—cafés, art galleries and terraces with views over the lower city. On summer Fridays, the Souk Jara market sets up here with local crafts and street food.

Final evening in Amman—the Jabal al-Weibdeh quarter, with its art galleries, literary cafés and restaurants in buildings from the 1930s–1950s, offers an atmosphere very different from the historic center. Perfect for a quiet dinner and an after-dinner stroll.

visits.text: Arrival in Aqaba, Jordan's only coastal city, situated at the country's extreme south on the Gulf of Aqaba. Don't expect a paradise beach downtown—the charm lies underwater. Start with the seafront (Corniche) and the Mamluk fort, built in the 14th century and reinforced by the Ottomans, which controlled the trade routes between Asia and Africa.

Head toward South Beach, 10 km south of downtown, at the heart of Aqaba Marine Park, which stretches along 7 km of coastline. With a mask and snorkel, you can reach a coral reef directly from shore—no boat needed. Here, the Red Sea is home to over 200 species of coral and more than 1,000 fish species: clownfish in their anemones, yellow-tailed surgeonfish, lionfish and moray eels. A few meters from shore, you can spot an M42 military tank deliberately submerged at a depth of 6 meters to create an artificial reef.

Continue 5 minutes north of South Beach to the Japanese Garden, considered by many to be the best snorkeling spot in Jordan. Its hard and soft corals with rounded shapes recall a Japanese garden. The depth doesn't exceed 12 meters and visibility often reaches 30 to 40 meters.

activities.text: Grilled fish dinner on Aqaba's seafront—souk or Corniche restaurants serve fresh Red Sea fish, accompanied by hummus and warm bread.

days_plan.itin_title: Jordan Road Trip: Petra, Wadi Rum & the Dead Sea

visits.text: Start the day at Mount Nebo, 8 km from Madaba; allow for a day trip from your accommodation on the Dead Sea. This promontory at an altitude of 817 m is where, according to Deuteronomy, Moses contemplated the Promised Land before dying at the age of 120. On a clear day, you will see the Dead Sea, the Jordan Valley and sometimes Jerusalem in the distance. In front of the restored basilica (fourth-century foundations, rebuilt in 597), admire the Brazen Serpent, a bronze sculpture by Gian Paolo Fantoni combining Christ's cross and Moses' serpent. Inside, mosaics dated to 530 show hunting and grape-harvesting scenes on a panel measuring 9 m by 3.

Allow for a day trip from your accommodation on the Dead Sea to visit Madaba. Open the door of Saint George's Church in Madaba, a modest Orthodox building erected in 1896 over the ruins of a sixth-century Byzantine basilica. It houses the Madaba Map, the oldest cartographic representation of the Holy Land—more than 2 million stone tesserae assembled around 550–560, originally measuring 21 m by 7 m (16 m by 5 remain). You will recognize Jerusalem in the center, the Dead Sea with two boats, and the Jordan with its fish. Arrive early in the morning—tour groups quickly crowd this small church.

Stay in Madaba for the archaeological park, a few streets from Saint George's; visit it as part of a day trip from your accommodation on the Dead Sea. You will see other Byzantine mosaics, including those of the Hippolytus Hall and the Church of the Virgin. Madaba is nicknamed the “city of mosaics” - if the subject fascinates you, you can join an introductory workshop at one of the craft studios that keep the tradition alive.

Late in the day, descend toward the Dead Sea—the lowest point on the planet, roughly 430 meters below sea level. The water contains nearly 30% salt (versus 3–4% in the oceans), making floating inevitable. Coat yourself with the black mud rich in magnesium and potassium, let it dry for 20 minutes, then rinse in the salty water. Don't exceed 20 minutes of bathing per session, and above all never put your head underwater. Bring water shoes because the salt crystals on the bottom are sharp.

activities.text: Sunset from the shores of the Dead Sea—the low-angle light on the calm waters and the mountains of the West Bank opposite. Bring a book for the classic souvenir photo: reading while floating.

days_plan.itin_title: Jordan Road Trip: Petra, Wadi Rum & the Dead Sea

visits.text: Set off early for Wadi Mujib, allowing for a day trip from Ma'in. The Siq Trail, nicknamed the “Grand Canyon of Jordan”, is a 3 km round-trip hike through water: you follow the river upstream between sandstone walls rising several dozen meters, with waist-deep water in places. The trail ends facing a waterfall. Allow 2 to 3 hours. Please note: restricted to visitors over 18, open only from April to October, closed in rainy weather. Bring a waterproof pouch for your phone and water shoes. Arrive as soon as it opens at 8 a.m. to avoid running into everyone on the way back.

After Mujib, head back up to the hot springs of Ma'in (Hammamat Ma'in). Waterfalls tumble down the wadi cliffs at temperatures that can reach 63 °C. The water is rich in sulfur, calcium and magnesium—Jordanians have bathed here for centuries, and tradition has it that King Herod the Great traveled from Jerusalem to treat his rheumatism. The natural pools at the foot of the waterfalls are accessible to everyone. After the cool canyon, the warmth of the springs makes a striking contrast.

On the route between Ma'in and the Dead Sea, detour to the Dead Sea Panoramic Complex. This viewpoint perched 400 meters above the shores offers a view down over the entire bluish expanse of the Dead Sea and the mountains opposite. A small museum traces the geological history and biodiversity of the region.

activities.text: Short hike in Wadi Zarqa Ma'in—a trail descending toward the waterfalls through a landscape of rock gorges and quasi-tropical vegetation, surprising in the middle of the desert.

days_plan.itin_title: Jordan Road Trip: Petra, Wadi Rum & the Dead Sea

visits.text: Enter Petra through the Siq, a 1.2-km canyon whose multicolored sandstone walls narrow to 3–4 meters wide. After a final turn, Al-Khazneh (the Treasury) appears: a 39-meter-high by 25-meter-wide façade carved from rose sandstone, probably a tomb for the Nabataean king Aretas IV (1st century BCE). The Bedouins believed an urn at the top held treasure and shot at it—the bullet impacts are still visible on this 3.5-meter urn carved from solid rock. Be there as soon as it opens, around 6–7 a.m., when the sun illuminates the façade and the stone turns bright pink—and especially before the groups arrive.

Continue beyond the Treasury to the Street of Facades, where about forty rock-cut tombs line the cliff face, then to the Nabataean theater carved from the sandstone, capable of seating around 3,000 spectators. Opposite, on the east cliff, the Royal Tombs merit the climb: the Urn Tomb offers a view down over the entire Petra valley. Estimates suggest only 10% of the site has been excavated to date.

Push on to the High Place of Sacrifice, accessible by a steep but short trail (20–30 min ascent). At the summit, a Nabataean altar carved from rock and a 360° view across Petra's mountains. The descent via Wadi Farasa lets you see less-frequented tombs and façades barely weathered by time.

End the day with the Colonnaded Street and Qasr al-Bint, one of Petra's rare built structures (not carved from rock)—probably a temple dedicated to the Nabataeans' principal deity. This is where French CNRS archaeologists conducted excavations that highlighted the city's urban character.

activities.text: Petra by Night: the Treasury lit by 1,500 candles, accompanied by Bedouin music and sage tea. Offered from Sunday to Thursday—inquire at the visitor center.

places.name: Wadi Rum

visits.text: Second day at Petra—head for the Monastery (Ad Deir). Climb the 800 steps from the central basin: the ascent takes 45 minutes to an hour, but at the summit you discover a façade 47 meters wide by 48 meters high, even more massive than the Treasury but in a far wilder setting. Bedouins run a small tea house directly opposite—take a break with a view. Descend by the same path or explore the trail to the viewpoint overlooking the valley.

On the way down toward the exit, stop at the Obelisk Tomb at the Siq entrance. It consists of two monuments, one above the other: above, four obelisks representing the deceased, and below, a triclinium (funerary banquet hall). If you have a bit of time, make a detour to Little Petra (Siq al-Barid), 10 minutes by car north of Wadi Musa—a mini-canyon with Nabataean façades and far fewer people.

In the afternoon, take the road to Wadi Rum (~1.5 hours from Wadi Musa). At the visitor center, board a 4x4 driven by a Bedouin guide. Wadi Rum, UNESCO-listed since 2011 (mixed natural and cultural site), covers 74,000 hectares of red sand and sandstone towers sometimes exceeding 1,800 meters. The circuit passes through Khazali Canyon, where 12,000-year-old petroglyphs show hunting scenes, then by the Um Fruth arch, easily accessible on foot. The desert has served as backdrop for Lawrence of Arabia, The Martian and other films.

Finish the 4x4 tour with a stop at sunset on a red dune in the south. When the low-angle light strikes the sandstone monoliths, the palette shifts from golden yellow to deep red in a few minutes. Complete silence, not a car, not a sound—it's the most powerful moment of the day.

activities.text: Night at a Bedouin camp in Wadi Rum—traditional tents or sleeping under the stars depending on the season. The zarb dinner (chicken and vegetables cooked in a sealed pit under the sand) is followed by sweet tea around the fire. Far from any light pollution, the night sky is spectacular—you'll make out the Milky Way with the naked eye.
